full_title: LOTRIM CONSTRUCTION, INC., REPRESENTED BY ITS PRESIDENT, ENGINEER ODILON MARLON L. GAVIOLA, AND ENGINEER ODILON MARLON L. GAVIOLA, PETITIONERS, VS. COMMISSION ON AUDIT, RESPONDENT.
subject: Political and Public International Law
syllabus_topic: VII. Constitutional Commissions > B. Civil Service Commission (CSC), Commission on Elections (COMELEC), and Commission on Audit (COA) > 2. Powers, Functions, and Jurisdiction
topics: COA Proper is not limited to the auditor's grounds (Yap v. COA)
Administrative due process in COA proceedings; TechITS inspection reports
Quantum meruit also allows the Government to recover overpayments
Rule 64 period: 30 days, and not less than five days after denial of reconsideration
Estoppel against belatedly invoking CIAC jurisdiction

other_subjects.subject: Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics
other_subjects.syllabus_topic: V. Special Civil Actions > D. Review of Commission on Elections and Commission on Audit Judgments and Final Orders or Resolutions (Rule 64)

other_subjects.subject: Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics
other_subjects.syllabus_topic: II. Jurisdiction > B. Subject Matter Jurisdiction > 2. Effect of Estoppel

doctrine:
**COA Proper is not limited to the grounds relied upon by the auditor** (*Yap v. COA*, reiterated). In the exercise of its constitutional audit power (Const., Art. IX-D, Sec. 2(2)), it must make its own assessment of a disallowance. It may adjust the amount, identify additional persons liable, or modify their participation without a separate audit observation memorandum, notice of suspension or notice of disallowance, provided the parties have a fair opportunity to be heard. Due process is satisfied where the party could explain its side or seek reconsideration. COA's Technical and Information Technology Services (TechITS) is an internal office answerable only to COA, so it need not notify the contractor of its inspection or furnish it its report.

**Quantum meruit cuts both ways.** It lets a contractor recover the reasonable value of work done under a void government contract. But it "cannot be distorted into a shield for contractors to retain payments in excess of what is legally or contractually due": the Government may recover payments that exceed the actual accomplishment. COA's factual findings on the amount due, if supported by substantial evidence, are respected.

Procedurally, under **Rule 64, Sec. 3**, the petition must be filed within 30 days from notice. A motion for reconsideration interrupts the period, and after its denial only the remaining period, but not less than five days, is left. A late petition makes the COA ruling final and immutable. Also, **a party who actively participated in the COA proceedings and sought affirmative relief is estopped from belatedly invoking CIAC jurisdiction** under an arbitration clause (*Tijam v. Sibonghanoy*; *Amoguis v. Ballado*).
facts:
In a December 20, 2012 public bidding for the expansion of the Administration Building of the Bureau of Customs (BOC) Port of Davao, Lotrim Construction, Inc. was declared the bidder with the lowest calculated and responsive bid, PHP 17,203,203.18. The approved budget for the contract was PHP 20,000,000.00. The contract was signed on March 15, 2013, and the notice to proceed was received on April 2, 2013. The BOC paid Lotrim a 15% advance payment of PHP 2,419,200.45 on April 12, 2013 and a first partial payment of PHP 3,828,184.10 on June 17, 2013.

COA disallowed the advance payment (ND dated July 12, 2013) and the partial payment (ND dated January 22, 2014). Its grounds were that maintenance and other operating expenses (MOOE) funds were diverted to new construction, contrary to PD 1445 and PD 1777. Funds had also been obligated on December 27, 2012 to a nonexistent creditor before any award, contrary to Book VI, Sec. 40 of EO 292, and FY 2011 savings had been spent beyond FY 2012. Lotrim was held liable as payee. The BOC ordered Lotrim to stop work, and Lotrim reported 80.67% accomplishment worth PHP 13,878,362.71. On the BOC's request, COA TechITS inspected the project. Its report dated April 7, 2014 found only 36.90% accomplishment, worth PHP 6,347,826.73.

The COA Cluster Director (October 7, 2015) lifted both NDs and allowed payment on *quantum meruit* up to the TechITS figure. On automatic review, COA Proper (Decision No. 2018-204, January 30, 2018) affirmed the NDs and held the contract void for lack of a valid appropriation. It held all persons named liable for PHP 6,247,384.55, but it limited Lotrim's liability to PHP 408,859.16: recomputing on *quantum meruit*, it found that Lotrim had been overpaid by that amount. It also ordered a supplemental ND against the BAC chairman and referred the matter to the Ombudsman.

Lotrim received the COA Proper decision on October 16, 2018 and moved for reconsideration on November 12, 2018. It attached a third-party report putting its accomplishment at 64.15% (PHP 12,131,455.56). COA denied the motion by Resolution No. 2022-010 dated January 28, 2022, which Lotrim received on August 31, 2023. Lotrim filed a Rule 64 petition on October 2, 2023. It claimed it was denied due process because the inspection was made without notice to it, and because the extent of its accomplishment should have been the subject of a separate audit observation memorandum, notice of suspension and notice of disallowance. It also claimed that the dispute belonged to the Construction Industry Arbitration Commission (CIAC).
issues: Whether the Rule 64 petition was filed on time.
Whether petitioners were denied due process when COA relied on the TechITS inspection, made without notice to them, and determined their accomplishment without a separate notice of disallowance.
Whether petitioners may invoke the jurisdiction of the CIAC at this stage.
Whether COA gravely abused its discretion in ordering petitioners to refund PHP 408,859.16 as an overpayment under quantum meruit.
disposition: Petition DISMISSED. COA Decision No. 2018-204 dated January 30, 2018 and Resolution No. 2022-010 dated January 28, 2022 were AFFIRMED. COA was DIRECTED to implement them and to collect the amounts overpaid to Lotrim Construction, Inc., consistent with *quantum meruit* and subject to applicable laws, rules and regulations.

bar_questions.q: BuildCo's contract with a government agency was declared void for lack of a valid appropriation, and the payments made to it were disallowed. On appeal, the COA Cluster Director allowed BuildCo to be paid on quantum meruit. On automatic review, COA Proper relied on an inspection report of its Technical and Information Technology Services (TechITS), which put BuildCo's actual accomplishment far below what it had billed. COA Proper found that BuildCo had been overpaid and ordered it to refund the excess. BuildCo was never notified of the inspection, but it attacked the inspection report in its motion for reconsideration, which COA Proper resolved on the merits. BuildCo argues that (i) it was denied due process, since the extent of its accomplishment should have been the subject of a separate notice of disallowance, and (ii) quantum meruit exists to protect contractors and cannot be used to make them refund. Rule on both arguments.

alac.answer: Both arguments fail. BuildCo was not denied due process, and quantum meruit may be the basis for ordering a contractor to refund an overpayment.
alac.legal_basis: Under Art. IX-D, Sec. 2(2) of the Constitution, COA has exclusive authority to define the scope of its audit and to disallow irregular or excessive expenditures. On appeal, COA Proper is not limited to the grounds relied upon by the auditor; it must make its own assessment and may adjust the amount disallowed or the persons liable, so long as the parties are given an opportunity to be heard (Yap v. COA). COA TechITS is an internal office that need not notify the contractor of its inspection or furnish it its report. Quantum meruit cuts both ways: it obliges the government to pay for benefits received but also allows recovery of overpayments. (Lotrim Construction, Inc. v. COA, G.R. No. 270295, April 29, 2026)
alac.application: (i) The extent of BuildCo's accomplishment was part and parcel of the audit of the disallowed payments, so no separate notice of disallowance was needed. The TechITS inspection was an internal technical aid to COA. BuildCo was heard: it attacked the report in its motion for reconsideration, and COA Proper ruled on it. That is all due process requires. (ii) BuildCo invoked quantum meruit to be paid for the reasonable value of its work. The same principle limits it to that value. Keeping payments beyond its actual accomplishment would unjustly enrich BuildCo at the public's expense.
alac.conclusion: COA Proper did not gravely abuse its discretion in ordering BuildCo to refund the overpayment.

bar_questions.q: Contractor Delta received a COA Proper decision on March 1. It moved for reconsideration on March 28. It received the resolution denying the motion on June 2 and filed a petition for certiorari under Rule 64 with the Supreme Court on July 2, without asking for an extension. (a) Was the petition filed on time? (b) If not, may the Supreme Court still correct a clear error in the computation of Delta's liability?

alac.answer: (a) No, the petition was late. (b) No. The COA ruling has become final and immutable, absent a compelling reason to relax the rules.
alac.legal_basis: Under Rule 64, Sec. 3 of the Rules of Court, a petition for certiorari against a COA judgment must be filed within 30 days from notice. A motion for reconsideration, if allowed by the COA rules, interrupts the period. If it is denied, the petitioner may file within the remaining period, which shall not be less than five days from notice of the denial. A late petition is fatal: the COA ruling becomes final, and under the doctrine of immutability it may no longer be modified, even to correct erroneous conclusions of fact or law. (Lotrim Construction, Inc. v. COA, G.R. No. 270295, April 29, 2026)
alac.application: (a) From March 1 to March 28, 27 of Delta's 30 days had run, leaving 3 days. Because the remaining period may not be less than five days, Delta had until June 7, five days from its June 2 receipt of the denial. Filing on July 2 was late. (b) Delta did not seek an extension, and no compelling reason to relax the rules appears. The COA decision therefore became final and immutable, and the Supreme Court can no longer modify it, even to correct an alleged error.
alac.conclusion: Delta's petition was filed out of time and should be dismissed, leaving the COA ruling final and unalterable.

bar_questions.q: Gamma's construction contract with a government agency provides that disputes shall be submitted to arbitration before the Construction Industry Arbitration Commission (CIAC). COA disallowed payments to Gamma and later found that Gamma had been overpaid. Gamma appealed to the COA Cluster Director and asked to be paid on quantum meruit. It then moved for reconsideration before COA Proper. It never mentioned arbitration in either proceeding. Only in its Rule 64 petition, nearly eight years after the Cluster Director's decision, did Gamma argue that COA had no jurisdiction to determine the extent of its accomplishment because that is a construction dispute cognizable by the CIAC. Will the argument prosper?

alac.answer: No. Gamma is estopped from invoking CIAC jurisdiction at this late stage.
alac.legal_basis: Issues not raised below cannot be raised for the first time on appeal, and a party may not change its theory on appeal. Under Tijam v. Sibonghanoy and Amoguis v. Ballado, a belated jurisdictional challenge is barred when six circumstances concur: the claimant had a statutory right; it did not invoke it; an unreasonable time passed before it raised jurisdiction; it actively participated and sought affirmative relief from the forum; it knew or should have known which forum had jurisdiction; and the other party would suffer irreparable damage after relying on the forum. CIAC jurisdiction, though generally available under an arbitration clause, is not absolute and may be waived by conduct. (Lotrim Construction, Inc. v. COA, G.R. No. 270295, April 29, 2026)
alac.application: Gamma had a contractual and statutory basis to seek CIAC arbitration but never invoked it. Instead, it actively litigated before COA and sought affirmative relief, namely quantum meruit payment and reconsideration. Gamma was a party to the arbitration clause, so it knew of the CIAC option. It raised the issue only after adverse rulings and after an unreasonable delay of almost eight years. Its conduct amounts to a waiver of CIAC jurisdiction and an implied submission to COA's.
alac.conclusion: Gamma's belated invocation of CIAC jurisdiction will not prosper.

notes: Promulgated April 29, 2026, within the June 30, 2026 cutoff. The main opinion adopts points raised by Associate Justices Lazaro-Javier (immutability) and Singh (the eight-year delay); both concurred, and these points are part of the main opinion. The body gives the disallowed payments as PHP 2,419,200.45 and PHP 3,828,184.10, totaling the PHP 6,247,384.55 liability. COA's overpayment computation, reproduced in footnote 36, uses gross figures (PHP 2,580,480.48 and PHP 5,568,341.04) less recoupment and retention. The decision says CIAC jurisdiction was first raised on September 29, 2023, although it records the petition as filed on October 2, 2023.
